text: This is the last lesson. Everything from here is one fictional company, walked through all five chapters of this course, in order — so you can see how the pieces actually fit together.

Meridian Fulfillment Co. — a fictional, illustrative company invented for this lesson, not a real business. Three systems hold a customer address field, nobody owns which one is authoritative, and shipments are going to the wrong place often enough that it's showing up in complaints. That one problem is the thread through every chapter.

Chapter one names this as a governance root cause behind a data quality symptom — trust and operational cost, not a compliance mandate. Chapter two says Meridian doesn't need the full DAMA-DMBOK treatment — just an operating-model decision: centralized enough to pick a winner when addresses disagree, federated enough to keep each business unit's day-to-day stewardship.

Chapter three's roles stop being abstract. A data owner — the operations director who already fields the complaints. A data steward — the analyst who already unofficially knows which records are suspect. A RACI that says who flags, who decides, who's consulted, who's informed. And an executive sponsor — the VP who raised this in the first place.

Chapter four doesn't need a full regulatory treatment here — there's no specific law driving this. It needs one policy naming the CRM as the authoritative source, one standard defining a valid address record, and one enforcement step: the other two systems sync from the CRM nightly instead of keeping independent copies.

Chapter five's full sequence, in order. Readiness: high pain, high sponsorship, low policy, low tooling. Business case: the problem, the scope, the resources, the anticipated value. Pilot: customer address data, a baseline complaint count, a ninety-day window. Roadmap: this pilot is days sixty-one through ninety of a longer plan. Communication: the sponsor frames it as how we stop shipping to the wrong address, not as a new rule to follow.

At day ninety, one number decides it: did address complaints actually drop against the baseline. If yes, the same five-step sequence repeats for the next domain. If not, the team checks which step broke down. The sequence doesn't change — only the domain does.

Congratulations — you've finished Data Governance Foundations. You now have the full sequence: what governance is, which frameworks and roles and policies make it real, and how to actually get a program funded, piloted, and heard. Next in the Data Governance path: Data Quality Management — where the quality side of this course gets its own full treatment.
